\label{ch:hi-letters-read-all-along}
\hlchaptermodality{128}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write the short i sign, the letter i and the letter nya, and find each one in a word I already say.}

Complete the last lesson of chapter 128: i can write the short i sign, the letter i and the letter nya, and find each one in a word I already say.

\section[i kī mātrā]{\hi{◌ि} (i kī mātrā) — the short i sign in \hi{शुक्रिया}}

\label{lesson:HI-W128-vowel-sign-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \hi{ड} and \hi{़} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\hi{शुक्रिया}} (\emph{shukriyā}), \textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{◌ि}}
\textbf{\hi{ि}} — the short \emph{i} sign.

It is inside \textbf{\hi{शुक्रिया}} (\emph{shukriyā}), \textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{}, one of the first words in this book. Look at \textbf{\hi{क्रि}}: the sign stands \textbf{before} the consonants and is said \textbf{after} them, \emph{kri}. It is the one Hindi vowel sign written ahead of the sound it follows.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{◌ि}}
Put your pen on \hi{◌ि} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start this letter or which way to travel}. It is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\hi{शुक्रिया}} and point at \hi{◌ि} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{◌ि} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{़}, then \hi{◌ि}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\hi{शुक्रिया}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \hi{◌ि}? (\textbf{i kī mātrā}, \emph{i}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\hi{शुक्रिया}}, \emph{shukriyā}, \textquotedblleft{}thanks\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\hi{इ} (i) — the letter inside \hi{दिखाइए}}

\label{lesson:HI-W128-letter-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \hi{़} and \hi{◌ि} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\hi{दिखाइए}} (\emph{dikhāie}), \textquotedblleft{}please show me\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{इ}}
\textbf{\hi{इ}} — the letter \emph{i}.

It is inside \textbf{\hi{दिखाइए}} (\emph{dikhāie}), \textquotedblleft{}please show me\textquotedblright{}. After \textbf{\hi{ा}} comes another vowel, and a vowel that follows a vowel has no consonant to ride on, so it is written as its own letter. \textbf{\hi{ि}}, from the last lesson, is the same vowel as a sign.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{इ}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/HI-W128-letter-i-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \hi{इ} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: descend the upright from the headline
  \item \textbf{2.} turn left and curve around the upper bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, sweep right through the waist and around the lower bowl
  \item \textbf{4.} finish down-right through the tail without lifting
  \item \textbf{5.} lift, then draw the shirorekha left-to-right — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \hi{इ} stroke order.svg’, panels 1–2, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\hi{दिखाइए}} and point at \hi{इ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{इ} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{◌ि}, then \hi{इ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\hi{दिखाइए}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \hi{इ}? (\textbf{i}, \emph{i}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\hi{दिखाइए}}, \emph{dikhāie}, \textquotedblleft{}please show me\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ña]{\hi{ञ} (ña) — the letter hidden inside \hi{ज्ञ}}

\label{lesson:HI-W128-letter-nya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \hi{◌ि} and \hi{इ} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\hi{संज्ञा}} (\emph{saṁjñā}), \textquotedblleft{}noun\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ञ}}
\textbf{\hi{ञ}} — \emph{ña}, a nasal made where \emph{j} is made.

It is hidden inside \textbf{\hi{संज्ञा}} (\emph{saṁjñā}), \textquotedblleft{}noun\textquotedblright{}. The joined letter \textbf{\hi{ज्ञ}} is \textbf{\hi{ज}} and \textbf{\hi{ञ}} written as one, and Hindi says the pair \emph{gy}. You have been reading \textbf{\hi{ञ}} inside that join without seeing it on its own.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ञ}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/HI-W128-letter-nya-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \hi{ञ} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: sweep clockwise around the open-left bowl
  \item \textbf{2.} lift, then sweep the shoulder right and rise to the headline
  \item \textbf{3.} lift, then descend the short lower stem
  \item \textbf{4.} lift, then draw the shirorekha left-to-right — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{ञ}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\hi{संज्ञा}} and point at \hi{ञ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ञ} three times, saying \emph{ñ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{इ}, then \hi{ञ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\hi{संज्ञा}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \hi{ञ}? (\textbf{ña}, \emph{ñ}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\hi{संज्ञा}}, \emph{saṁjñā}, \textquotedblleft{}noun\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
